big: Rohan can only spare ₹10,000 a month. He knows his salary will grow. This is what happens if his SIP grows with it.

lines: I can only invest ₹10,000 now. But my salary will rise every year. Is a flat SIP enough?
Let us give the SIP a staircase. Raise it 10% each year, and watch what ten years does.

alt: Ten bars of yearly instalment rising 10% a year against a flat dashed line
caps: Year 1. Both SIPs start at ₹10,000 a month.
Each year the green step rises 10%. The dashed line is the flat SIP.
By year 10 the instalment is ₹23,579 a month.
At an assumed 12% a year, the flat SIP reaches about ₹23 lakh and the step-up about ₹33 lakh. An illustration, not a promise.

alt: Two bars: money put in and final value, flat against step-up
caps: The step-up put in ₹7.1 lakh more over ten years.
That extra money, invested while income was higher, is most of the gap. The step gives you a habit, not a better fund.

q: Rohan's 10% step-up SIP ends ten years about ₹10 lakh ahead of his flat SIP. What explains most of that gap?
opts: Step-up SIPs earn a higher rate of return than flat SIPs in the same fund
It invests about ₹7 lakh more, and the extra goes in as income rises
Banks pay a loyalty bonus when the instalment rises every single year
The fund house waives its expense ratio on the extra stepped-up amount
why: Return depends on the fund, not on how the instalment is set. Both SIPs here earn the same assumed rate.
Total invested is ₹19.1 lakh against ₹12 lakh. More money working for longer is where most of the gap comes from.
No such bonus exists. Banks only run the mandate, and the instalment size has no effect on any payout.
Expense ratio is charged on the whole fund value either way. There is no waiver for a stepped-up amount.

q: A client earns ₹40,000 a month and expects raises of about 6% a year. He asks for a 25% yearly step-up to build wealth faster. What do you say?
opts: Agree to 25%, since a bigger step always builds a bigger corpus for him
Suggest a step near his raises, 5 to 8% a year, and review it yearly
Tell him step-ups are only meant for people who earn above ₹1 lakh a month
Suggest a flat SIP instead, because any step-up adds extra risk to the fund
why: A step he cannot keep up leads to missed instalments, and a stopped SIP gives a smaller corpus than a modest step.
A step near his income growth feels light, so he is likely to keep it. The yearly review lets him adjust.
Step-ups work at any income. What matters is that the step fits the cash he really has to spare.
A step-up changes how much goes in, not what the fund holds. It adds no risk beyond the fund's own.

q: Rohan starts at ₹10,000 a month and steps up by 10% each year. What is his monthly instalment in year 4?
why: ₹13,000 adds ₹1,000 a year to the first amount. A step-up of 10% grows on the latest instalment each time.
₹14,000 treats the step as 10% a year for four full years on the first amount, which counts one year too many.
Each year multiplies by 1.10: ₹11,000, then ₹12,100, then ₹13,310 in year 4. The steps compound.
₹12,100 is the year 3 figure. Year 1 has no step, so year 4 has taken three steps, not two.

q: Which risk comes from setting the yearly step too high?
opts: Missed instalments when cash is tight, which can stop the SIP
A lower NAV on the units bought later in the year
The fund house cancelling the mandate for being too large
A higher tax rate on the gains from the larger instalments
why: A bounced or skipped instalment breaks the habit, and repeated misses can cancel the SIP, so the corpus falls short.
NAV follows the market, not the size of the instalment. A larger step does not change the price you pay.
Fund houses accept any amount above the minimum. They do not cancel a mandate for being too large.
Tax depends on how long you hold and the gain made, not on how big each instalment was.

pts: Step up with income, in small steps you can sustain.
Most of the extra corpus comes from putting more money in.
Review the step every year, with the goal.
